- 1 medium yellow onion, sliced into half-moons
- 5 cloves garlic, minced (divided)
- 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for the tomatoes
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, divided
- 1/2 cup (100g) long-grain white rice
- 3/4 cup low-sodium chicken broth
- 1/2 cup frozen mixed vegetables (peas, carrots, corn)
- 1 teaspoon dried thyme
- 1 teaspoon dried rosemary
- 1/2 teaspoon dried sage
- 1 can (14.5 oz) whole peeled tomatoes, drained and roughly chopped
- Diamond Crystal kosher salt
- Freshly ground black pepper

*Chef’s Note: If you have fresh herbs, double the amounts and use them—fresh thyme and sage turn this into a special-occasion dish without adding a single minute of work.*

### Step 1: Preheat and Season the Chicken

Set an oven rack to the middle position and preheat to 400°F (204°C). While the oven climbs, pat the easy [easy 4 ingredient chicken breast recipes](/recipes/easy-4-ingredient-chicken-breast-recipes) [healthy dinner ideas for two recipes](/recipes/easy-4-ingredient-chicken-breast-recipes)s thoroughly dry with paper towels—this is non-negotiable if you want skin that crackles rather than steams. Rub each breast all over with 1 tablespoon of the olive oil, then season generously with salt, pepper, the thyme, rosemary, and sage. I use about 1/2 teaspoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt per breast; if you’re using Morton’s, cut that by a third.

In a medium bowl, toss the onion slices and half of the minced garlic with the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and a pinch of salt. Spread this mixture in the center of a rimmed sheet pan, creating a bed for the chicken.

### Step 2: Build the Sheet Pan

Nestle the chicken breasts skin-side up on top of the onion-garlic mixture. Make sure the pieces aren’t touching—airflow is what gives you that golden, shattery skin. Slide the pan into the oven and set a timer for 25 minutes.

**USDA Minimum Temperature: 165°F / 74°C for poultry.** Check the thickest part of the breast with an instant-read thermometer; the temperature will continue to rise 3–5°F during resting, so pull it at exactly 160°F if you want a final 165°F. Note: the onion rings should be deeply browned and jammy at the edges. If they’re still pale by the time the healthy dinner recipes for 2 hits temperature, give them another 5 minutes on their own—you want that caramelization for the pan sauce.

### Step 3: Cook the Rice Pilaf

While the sheet pan roasts, melt 1 tablespoon of the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the remaining minced garlic and cook just until fragrant, about 30 seconds—stop before it colors. Stir in the rice and cook, stirring constantly, until the grains turn opaque and smell nutty, roughly 1 minute. This toasting step distinguishes pilaf from boiled rice; it coats each grain in fat so they stay separate and firm.

Pour in the chicken broth and bring to a boil. Cover, reduce the heat to low, and simmer for 15 minutes. Then scatter the frozen vegetables on top (no need to stir), cover again, and cook 5 more minutes. Turn off the heat and let the pot sit, covered, for 5 minutes to finish steaming. Fluff with a fork, season with salt and pepper, and dot with the remaining 1 tablespoon butter.

**Chef Augustin’s Tip:** Frozen vegetables release moisture, so adding them on top without stirring minimizes mush. They steam gently while the rice finishes absorbing liquid. It’s a tiny detail that keeps individual peas intact instead of turning them into green smears.

### Step 4: Prepare the Tomato Salad

While both the chicken and rice are cooking, tip the drained tomatoes onto a cutting board and give them a rough chop—you want pieces about the size of a walnut half. In a small bowl, toss them with a glug of olive oil, the remaining pinch of minced garlic, and a grind of black pepper. Let this sit at room temperature; the salt will draw out the tomato juices and create its own simple dressing.

Canned whole tomatoes are the unsung hero of the off-season kitchen. San Marzano-style tomatoes, packed in their own juice, hold more flesh and less water than diced versions, so they behave almost like fresh plum tomatoes when dressed simply. I’ve put this salad next to a roasted chicken on a Tuesday and had guests ask if I was growing tomatoes in December.

### Step 5: Rest and Slice the Chicken

When the chicken reaches temperature, transfer the breasts to a cutting board and tent loosely with foil. Let them rest for 5 full minutes—this redistributes the juices so you don’t leave the best part of the meal on the cutting board. While the chicken rests, scrape the caramelized onion and garlic from the sheet pan into a small bowl; you’ll spoon these over the final plate.

Slice each breast against the grain into thick medallions. If the skin is crisp (it should be), leave it attached—it will shatter under a fork.

### Step 6: Plate the Feast

Mound the rice pilaf onto two warm plates. Fan the sliced chicken beside it, then spoon the reserved caramelized onion-garlic mixture over the top, catching any brown bits from the pan. Add a generous spoonful of tomato salad on the side, drizzling its juices wherever they land.

What a turkey dinner takes hours to promise, this delivers in under an hour: rich, savory meat, a buttery starch, and a sharp, acidic counterpoint that cuts through every bite.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong

The biggest mistake I see in small-format Thanksgiving recipes is treating the meal like a checklist: turkey, stuffing, potatoes, cranberry, pie. That’s fine for 12 people, but for two, it becomes a kind of holiday performance anxiety. The real goal is a plate that *feels* like Thanksgiving—with the same warmth, the same aromas, and the same permission to eat slowly and talk—without leaving the cook exhausted.

Many recipes also skip the technical details. They’ll say “roast until done” without giving an internal temperature, or they’ll assume everyone knows that rest time matters. My sheet-pan method makes the temperature the star, because food safety and texture are the same thing when you’re working with poultry. 165°F / 74°C isn’t just a rule—it’s the exact point where the muscle fibers have tightened enough to hold moisture and the collagen has softened, and I’ve never once regretted checking it.

## Chef’s Tips & What I’ve Learned

**Chef Augustin’s Tip: Salt the chicken 30 minutes ahead.** If you can spare the time, season the chicken breasts and let them sit uncovered in the fridge for 30 minutes before cooking. This dry-brine effect deepens the seasoning and tightens the skin, so it renders more fat and gets impossibly crisp. I’ve tested side-by-side, and even 20 minutes makes a visible difference.

**Chef Augustin’s Tip: Save the tomato juice.** When you drain the canned tomatoes, capture the liquid in a bowl. It’s a bright, slightly acidic broth that I’ll sometimes whisk into the pan sauce or use to deglaze a skillet. On a holiday, it might become a quick vinaigrette. Waste nothing.

A good sheet pan knows its own corners: keep the chicken toward the center where the oven’s heat is most even, and let the onion fill the edges where it can char without burning.

## FAQ

### Can I use frozen chicken breasts?

I don’t recommend it for this recipe. Frozen breasts release so much water as they thaw that the skin won’t crisp, and the cooking time becomes unpredictable. If frozen is your only option, thaw them completely in the refrigerator overnight, then pat them obsessively dry—use 4 paper towels instead of 2. The oven can only brown what’s dry; anything wet simply steams. I’ve tried it once on a deadline, and the result was edible but not proud.

### What if I can’t find skin-on chicken breasts?

Skin-on breasts are worth searching for because the fat bastes the meat from above while rendering into a crisp shell. If you can only find skinless, reduce the oven temperature to 375°F (190°C) and brush the tops with melted butter mixed with a little Dijon mustard to help a semblance of browning. The internal temperature target remains the same. It won’t be identical, but it’ll still taste like a proper holiday dinner.

### Can I make the pilaf ahead?

Yes, and it’s a smart move if you want to minimize last-minute work. Cook the pilaf, spread it on a plate to cool quickly, and refrigerate it in an airtight container for up to 24 hours. Reheat it gently in the microwave with a splash of broth, or crisp it in a hot skillet with a little butter. I’ve done the skillet version on Thanksgiving morning and the crispy bits were better than the original.

### What if I want a more traditional turkey?

You can swap in a single bone-in turkey breast (about 2 pounds) for the two chicken breasts. Increase the roasting time to 50–60 minutes, but check the temperature at 45 minutes. The target is still 165°F / 74°C at the thickest point. A turkey breast has more mass and takes longer to come to temperature, so tent it loosely with foil if the skin browns too quickly. Everything else stays the same.

### Why canned tomatoes over fresh in a salad?

In November, fresh tomatoes taste of refrigeration and disappointment. Canned whole San Marzano tomatoes are picked and packed at peak ripeness, so they’re sweeter and more complex than anything the grocery store offers outside of August. Draining them well is crucial; I let them sit in a sieve for 5 minutes before chopping. This salad has become one of my most requested holiday sides, and no one guesses its pantry origin until I tell them.

### Can I cook the rice on the sheet pan too?

I’ve tested it, and the answer is no—not without a lot more liquid and careful spacing that complicates the simplicity. Rice needs steady moisture and steam, which a 400°F oven evaporates too aggressively. A separate saucepan gives you control and keeps the sheet pan from overcrowding. When I care enough to make a holiday dinner, I care enough to wash one extra pot.

The table, when I set it, is small: two plates, two forks, a candle if we’re feeling ceremonial. The steam from the chicken rises while the last of the tomato salad’s juice pools on the plate, and for a few minutes, there’s nothing else to do but eat and be quiet together. That’s what a Thanksgiving for two actually looks like.

garlic-butter-chicken-pasta-for-two.content_markdown:
# 20-Minute Garlic Butter Chicken Pasta for Two

Dinner for two shouldn't require three pans and a sink full of regret. Tonight it's one skillet, one pot of pasta, and about twenty minutes from cold chicken to a plate you'll want to photograph. Most "quick dinner for two" roundups online give you a *list* of ideas — Alfredo, quesadillas, tuna melts — but skip the one thing [that actually](/recipes/recipes-for-two) makes weeknight cooking fast: cooking the protein and the sauce in the *same* pan so the fond does the work for you. That's the difference. Every brown bit stuck to the skillet after searing chicken is free flavor, and I'm going to show you how to spend it.

This is the meal I make when it's 6:40 p.m., we're both hungry, and neither of us wants to "decide." It scales cleanly to two portions (no sad leftover half-recipe), and the sauce comes together while the pasta boils. That's the whole trick to fast cooking for two — overlapping tasks, not rushing them.

## Why This Works

The magic is the fond — those caramelized brown bits left in the pan after you sear the chicken. When you sear chicken breast in a hot skillet, the Maillard reaction (the chemistry of browning that kicks in around 300°F / 150°C) builds hundreds of flavor compounds on the meat's surface and on the pan itself. If you wipe that pan and start a sauce from scratch, you've thrown that flavor away. Instead, I deglaze: I pour liquid into the hot pan and scrape the fond loose so it dissolves into the sauce.

I've tested this deglazing step with both water and canned tomato liquid, and the tomatoes win by a mile — their acidity lifts the fond faster and adds body. According to USDA guidance, chicken breast is safe at an internal temperature of 165°F / 74°C, and searing then finishing in the sauce gets you there without drying the meat out, because the sauce insulates it during the last few minutes. Fast doesn't have to mean rubbery.

[Garlic butter](/recipes/dinner-recipe-ideas-for-two) is doing double duty too. Butter is an emulsion of fat and water; when you melt it into the pasta at the end with a splash of starchy pasta water, it forms a glossy sauce that clings to every noodle. That's why I always save a mug of pasta water before draining.

## Ingredients

Everything here is a weeknight pantry regular — nothing you have to hunt for. The chicken breast is the star, so buy the best you can; a fresh, plump breast sears far better than a watery frozen-then-thawed one (though thawed works in a pinch — just pat it very dry). Garlic should be fresh cloves, not the jarred stuff, because jarred garlic turns bitter when it hits a hot pan. Canned tomatoes give you a fast sauce with real depth — I keep whole peeled tomatoes and crush them by hand for texture. The frozen vegetables are your shortcut to something green on the plate without any chopping; peas or a pea-and-corn mix melt right into the sauce.

If you're out of pasta, this works over rice too (start the rice first, since it takes longer). And if you only have [ground beef](/recipes/easy-beef-ramen-noodle-recipes), brown it instead of searing chicken — I'll tell you how in the FAQ. Whatever you swap, the garlic-butter-tomato base carries it.

## Instructions

### Step 1: Boil the Pasta
Get a pot of salted water going before you touch the chicken — this is the overlap that makes the whole dinner fast. Salt it like the sea (about 1 tablespoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt per quart).

### Step 2: Sear the Chicken
Pat the chicken breast bone-dry (wet chicken steams, it doesn't sear) and cook it in a hot skillet until deeply golden. You want an internal temperature of 165°F / 74°C for safety. Don't move it for the first three minutes — let the crust form.

### Step 3: Rest and Slice
Pull the chicken to a plate to rest while you build the sauce. It'll keep cooking a touch from residual heat.

### Step 4: Deglaze
This is the money step. Pour the canned tomatoes into the same hot pan and scrape every brown bit loose with a wooden spoon. That fond is your flavor.

### Step 5: Simmer the Sauce
Let the tomatoes reduce and stir in the frozen vegetables — they'll thaw and cook in the hot sauce in about two minutes.

### Step 6: Marry Everything
Add the drained pasta, the sliced chicken, garlic butter, and a splash of pasta water. Toss until glossy.

**Chef Augustin's Tip:** Finish the pan off the heat with the last knob of butter. Butter added off-heat emulsifies into a silky coat instead of breaking into greasy pools — the difference between a sauce that *clings* and one that *slides*.

A hot pan and a dry surface are worth more than any expensive ingredient.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong

Most "fast dinner for two" articles treat speed as a *list problem* — here are 15 ideas, pick one. But the real bottleneck on a weeknight isn't deciding, it's *dishes and dead time*. Almost none of them teach you to cook the protein and the sauce in the same pan, which is the single biggest time-and-flavor saver in home cooking. They tell you to make a sauce and cook chicken separately, then combine — two pans, two cleanups, and you've discarded the fond.

The other miss: nobody mentions saving pasta water. I've watched people drain pasta straight down the sink and then wonder why their sauce won't stick. That cloudy, starchy water is liquid gold for emulsifying a quick sauce.

## Chef's Tips & What I've Learned

**Chef Augustin's Tip:** Slice the chicken *against* the grain. The muscle fibers run in one direction; cutting across them shortens each fiber so every bite is tender instead of stringy. On a chicken breast the grain usually runs lengthwise, so slice crosswise.

**Chef Augustin's Tip:** If your sauce tastes flat, it's almost always missing salt or acid — not more herbs. A final pinch of salt or a squeeze of lemon wakes the whole pan up. I keep a lemon by the stove for exactly this.

Cooking for two is the easiest number to cook for — small pans heat fast and nothing gets lost in the crowd.

I've made this in both a nonstick and a stainless skillet. Stainless gives you better fond (and therefore a better sauce), but nonstick is more forgiving if your chicken sticks. Use what you have.

## Frequently Asked Questions

## What is the easiest fastest dinner for two?
A one-pan protein-and-sauce dish like this is my answer. Because the pasta boils while the chicken sears and the sauce comes together in the same skillet, active time is around 20 minutes with only two vessels to wash. The key is overlapping tasks — start the water first, sear while it boils, and build the sauce in the pan you already dirtied. Speed comes from sequencing, not from cutting corners on flavor.

## Can I use ground beef instead of chicken?
Absolutely, and it's actually faster. Skip the searing-and-resting steps and instead brown 8 oz (225g) ground beef in the skillet, breaking it up as it cooks, until it reaches an internal temperature of 160°F / 71°C. Drain off excess fat, then deglaze with the canned tomatoes right in the same pan. The fond from browned beef makes an even richer sauce. Everything else stays the same — same pasta, same garlic butter finish.

## How do I feed two people cheaply with this?
This recipe already leans budget-friendly: one chicken breast, half a box of pasta, a can of tomatoes, and frozen vegetables run a few dollars total. To stretch it further, swap the chicken for two eggs stirred in at the end, or bulk it out with an extra handful of frozen vegetables. Rice is cheaper than pasta per serving if you're counting pennies. The garlic-butter-tomato base is forgiving enough to carry whatever protein is on sale.

## Why is my chicken dry?
Almost always overcooking. Chicken breast is safe at 165°F / 74°C, but every extra minute past that squeezes out moisture. Use an instant-read thermometer and pull the breast the moment it hits temperature, then let it rest — resting lets the juices redistribute instead of running onto the cutting board. Searing over high heat and finishing briefly in the sauce also helps, because the sauce shields the meat from direct heat during the last few minutes.

## Can I make this ahead of time?
You can, but it's best fresh. The pasta absorbs sauce as it sits, so leftovers tighten up. Store cooled portions in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth and warm gently on the stove — this loosens the sauce back to its original glossy texture. I don't recommend freezing; the tomato sauce holds fine but cooked pasta turns mushy after thawing.

By the time you sit down, the kitchen still smells like garlic and browned butter, there are exactly two forks and one pan in the sink, and the pasta is still steaming on the plate between you.
